Zero Waste Living [5007]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Annually South Africa dumps 108 million tonnes of waste in landfills. We are rapidly running out of space and the only solution is recycling and reducing the amount of packaging we buy.

To lessen our impact on the environment we are encouraged to reduce reuse and recycle but are we really doing this effectively. Is it making a difference.

The difference is easy to see when someone goes hard core.

When the garbage collector comes to collect garbage there is nothing to pick up at Bea Johnson’s home in California. In fact she is so good at living what she has termed a Zero Waste lifestyle that her family generates a glass jar of rubbish a year.

The chic French woman has been dubbed “The Priestess of Waste-Free Living” by The New York Times and the “Messiah of Ecology” by Paris Match. She has inspired followers of her ideals to open zero waste restaurants in the UK and zero waste stores around Europe and has addressed the European Parliament and the United Nations.

It is estimated that on average each person in the world dumps around 438kg of waste annually. Globally, 1.3 billion tons of waste is generated each year

What has become a global movement is based on her five principles. “Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Rot - and only in that order,” she says. She has inspired thousands of people around the world to live simply and take a stand against needless waste. Her philosophy? “Own less, waste less and live more.”

.Zero waste is not the preserve of hippies, she says, you can be stylish while saving time, money and the planet. Even though she restricts herself to a 15 piece wardrobe of second-hand clothing that fits into an airplane carry-on bag, she writes a popular fashion blog and also gives hints and tips on how to create your own makeup. Her book, Zero Waste Home has been translated into 12 languages.
Her life of “voluntary simplicity” has allowed her family to save so much money that they can now afford the things they never thought possible.

Colleen Black was so inspired by Bea Johnson’s story that she also adopted a Zero Waste philosophy in Ballito near Durban and says that it is not as hard as it seems. She runs a blog about her adventures and manages to keep her waste down to a small bucketful a year.

She is willing to take us through a day in her life looking at how to reduce our impact on the environment.

What both individuals are very vocal about is using single use plastic items like straws. 175 billion plastic straws go into landfill sites every year. Hayley McLellen who has the NGO “Rethink the Bag” in Cape Town is passionate about educating people about the impact of plastic and single use items. I have also been in touch with her. The Cape Town Aquarium where she works bans plastic bags from coming into the Aquarium and they don’t provide any at their gist shop.
She is a passionate campaigner against reducing plastic consumption.

While we have had stories on reducing and recycling before, Bea Johnson takes this to a new level that our audiences haven’t seen before. She is very sophisticated and very eloquent.

Interviews: Bea Johnson will be in Durban on the 8th of May
Colleen Black lives in Ballito and will take us through a day in her life
Waste Mangement specialist
Environmentalist
Hayley McLellan Rethink the Bag

We have been given permission to use a video that Bea has of her at home and how she reduces her environmental footprint.
We will also get visuals of landfill sites and recycling plants.






The other factor is the environmental impact all of the packaging has on the environment.

Press Release:


Zero Waste Living
When the garbage collector comes to Bea Johnson’s home in California, there’s always nothing to collect. Dubbed “The Priestess of Waste-Free
Living”, her family of four astonishingly generate just a single glass jar of rubbish every year. Carte Blanche finds out how she does it.

Script:


Zero Waste Script


V/O
Labelled as a throw away society, we are all aware of the global pollution problem, but it’s a subject we prefer to ignore.

These portraits by photographer Gregg Segal are a shocking/unforgettable account of the amount of rubbish that these American families accumulated in just 7 days. But we are no different.

Link (Presenter to camera)
The average South African generates 1 ton of waste per year, that’s about 3 kg per person per day or one bag per person per week.

V/O
In contrast, this glass jar of household waste contains a few toothbrush bristles, a bar code sticker and a yellow baloon. Bea Johnson says this is her 2016 jar.

Bea
“There are fruit and vegestickers, they must be in there, I just don’t know where they are but they are in there.”

Bongani
“That’s a year’s worth of waste?”

Bea
“Yes, that 2016, that’s year’s worth of waste for a family of four.”

Bongani
“That’s incredible.”

Bea
“You can do it.”

V/O
This is not an anomaly Bea has been living what she calls a Zero Waste Lifestyle. And these jars are the sum total of her household waste over 5 years.

V/O
So how does she do it? Bea says she does not buy into consumerism. She takes her own jars to the supermarkets and they are filled up at the deli counter and she refuses the plastic bags and packaging.


Up sound margesses until turn jar and fill it.



V/O
Bea was born in France but now lives in San Franscisco, her environmental awkening started when
her family wanted to live closer to the city and sold their home. They put their belongings in storage for a year while they house hunted.

Bea
“When we did find a right house in the downtown. We got everything out of storage and we found that 80% of the belongings that we put in there we hadn’t even missed for a whole year. So we let go of it. It took a while but little by little we let go of about 80% .

V/O
As a family they have certainly embraced minimalism. This is their wardrobe, all of them can fit their clothes into one suitcase.

Bea
“In a typical wardrobe people only use 20% of their clothes, they typically keep the other 80% for the what if. What if I need it or loose weight or gain weight we have lots of reasons why we hang onto these things.”

V/O
But they didn’t stop at paring down their posessions they starting researching their impact on the environment around them.

Bongani
“Have you always been environmentally conscious?

Bea
“No really not. It’s reading those books and watching those documentaries that give us an idea that it was about time that we did something about children future we just felt bad for the future we were creating for them and we decided to take action.”

V/O
And this jar of waste is testament to her zeal to adopt a lifestyle that is less harmful to the environment.

V/O
Although her jar is a little fuller than Bea’s, Colleen Black in/from Ballito has also converted to a simpler lifestyle.

Colleen Black
“I’ve always been into green living and when I stumbled across the term zero waste living I realised that I wasn’t green at all. You think if you use eco friendly products then you are green but they are also packaged and full of chemicals and I realised I wasn’t.”

V/O
Colleen says adopting this lifestyle was not only an obvious but also an ethical choice to make and says she has never looked back.

Bongani
“So how did you begin?”

Colleen
“We stopped buying packaged processed food, so we didn’t buy anything packaged in plastic. We only bought fruit and vegetables that were unpackaged. I found a place that we could get our milk in reusable containers and same with cheeses. Lots of things you can buy over the counter, olives, any deli products we would shop that way.”

Link
Bea’s first point of call is to refuse, not to reduce , not to recycle but refuse. Say no to what you don’t need, no to junk mail, no to single use items, no to freebies, she believes that by accepting them we create a demand for more.

V/O
It’s as simple as using re usable bags for buying fruits and vegetables,avoiding products packaged in plastic and composting what you can. Her family will even go so far that her boys taking their own plates for take out pizza, instead of it being packaged in a cardboard box that is only used once and then goes to the landfill.


Bea
“It’s very important to understand that when you buy a single use item, it’s not only depleting the environment of natural resources, very few items have the chance of being recycled. When you buy a single use item so you buy it you use it you throw it away, its literally throwing your money away.”

Link
She argues that most of what we consume we don’t need and so by stepping away from this culture of masss consumerism she has saved 40% on her house hold budget.

V/O
Through this journey Bea started a blog, wrote a book and Zero Waste has gained traction internationally, she has been called the Waste Priestess and thousands of people around the world are now taking personal responsibility for their waste.

V/O
When you consider that it takes about 450 years for a plastic bottle to degrade , the environmental impact of our waste will be here for tens of generations to come.




Raymond
“I think that people don’t understand the amount of energy in handling and treating waste.”

V/O
Raymond Rampersad is head of Solid Waste in Durban and says that South Africa spends 17 billion rands on treating waste in our country and he fully supports the idea of reducing and recycling our resources. Currently Only 27% of South Africans recycle their waste.

Raymond
“There has to be a paradigm shift in how you view waste. My take is that if you change that and we are successful in educating the public at large to rather look at waste as a resource and to create jobs and to look after our environment for years to come I think we are in the right direction.”

V/O
So apart from refusing plastic, Colleen also has cut down on cleaning products, she also found 1 organic product that they wash everything with including the dog.


Colleen
“I think we can all make a difference, you don’t have to go the whole route and change your lifestyle if that is not for you. Just start off with one small thing and it will just progress and you can make small changes that will make a difference.”

V/O
Some may see the Zero Waste Lifestyle as extreme. It’s certainly simplified .This is Bea ‘s family’s whole cosmetic cabinet, they use a salt crystal deoderant and bicarb for toothpaste and a bioderadable soap for their bodies.

Bea
“People tend to think that if I am able to live a Zero Waste lifestyle I am a stay at home mom with way too much time on my hands. I think they picture that I spend my days worrying about my trash and making a bunch of things that’s not the case at all. I make very very few things.

V/O
She also makes her own eyeliner and mascara and uses cocoa powder for her blusher and beetroot for her lipstick.

Bongani
“What do you think your impact has been on the environment?”

Colleen
“I think we have made a huge difference. Just look down the road on a Monday and Thursday and see all the black bins going out . Do the best that we can, we are far from perfect. We still buy things occassionally we will buy things that are packaged. So we just do our best and that all any of us can do.”





V/O
Both Colleen and Bea have said that while it is rewarding that they have lessened their impact on the environment. The one advantage of living simply is that it has enhanced their quality of life with their families.

Bea
‘That’s truly the best advantage is discovering an improved life, its discovering a life that is based on experiences instead of things, a life based on being instead of having that is what makes life richer.”


Promo 1

This family of four posed with the amount of waste they generated in one week. But this families yearly waste fits into a jar. It’s called Zero Waste Living.

Promo 2

Bongani
“That’s a year’s worth of waste?”
Bea
“Yes, that 2016, that’s year’s worth of waste for a family of four.”
Bongani
“That’s incredible.”
V/O
Bea Johnson has been called the Waste Priestess and her Zero Waste Living movement is gaining global momentum.


Promo 3



Link
The average South African generates 1 ton of waste per year that about one bag per person per week.

V/O ( Fast Read)
So how does a family of four fit their yearly household waste into this little jar. Meet the Johnsons who practise Zero Waste Living.
Promo 4

These people posed for these photographs with just a week’s worth of household waste they had collected.
The Johnson’s live a Zero Waste Lifestyle and these are their sum total of household waste they collected over 4 years.

Her life of “voluntary simplicity” has allowed her family to save so much money that they can now afford the things they never thought possible. Colleen Black was so inspired by Bea Johnson’s story that she also adopted a Zero Waste philosophy in Ballito near Durban and says that it is not as hard as it seems. She runs a blog about her adventures and manages to keep her waste down to a small bucketful a year. She is willing to take us through a day in her life looking at how to reduce our impact on the environment. What both individuals are very vocal about is using single use plastic items like straws. 175 billion plastic straws go into landfill sites every year. Hayley McLellen who has the NGO “Rethink the Bag” in Cape Town is passionate about educating people about the impact of plastic and single use items. I have also been in touch with her. The Cape Town Aquarium where she works bans plastic bags from coming into the Aquarium and they don’t provide any at their gist shop. She is a passionate campaigner against reducing plastic consumption. While we have had stories on reducing and recycling before, Bea Johnson takes this to a new level that our audiences haven’t seen before. She is very sophisticated and very eloquent. We will also get visuals of landfill sites and recycling plants. The other factor is the environmental impact all of the packaging has on the environment.
